planting.note: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container stock in spring into deep, well-drained soil, giving it generous room for its eventual wide, dense canopy.

directions: European beech is the stately European species behind the many purple-leaved, weeping, and columnar named cultivars already grown as ornamental shade trees, carrying smooth gray bark and glossy, wavy-edged green leaves that often persist tan and papery through winter on young trees. It forms a dense, broadly oval canopy that casts deep shade, shading out most understory plants beneath mature specimens. Plant in full sun to light shade on deep, moist, well-drained soil, avoiding compacted or waterlogged sites that stress its shallow, wide-spreading root system. It is slow to establish but extremely long-lived, often remaining a centerpiece of a landscape for a century or more.
sources: USDA Forest Service Silvics of North America

planting.note: Sow in early spring or late summer for fall bloom into moist, well-drained soil; it performs best where summers stay mild.

directions: English daisy is the European wild-type species behind the double, pompon-flowered named selections such as 'Pomponette' already sold as bedding plants, bearing simple white, pink-tipped single flowers over a low rosette of spoon-shaped leaves in its unimproved form. It naturalizes readily in lawns and meadows in cool, moist climates, often treated as a cheerful weed in regions with mild summers. Grow it in full sun to light shade on consistently moist, well-drained soil, and expect it to struggle or go dormant through hot, humid summers. In favorable climates it self-sows and can act as a short-lived perennial rather than a strict annual.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into well-drained soil in full sun, allowing room for its slow but eventually substantial pyramidal form.

directions: Swiss stone pine is the Alpine European species behind the dwarf and narrow named selections such as 'Herman' already grown, forming a dense, narrow pyramid of soft, blue-green five-needle clusters that holds its tidy shape with age. It is exceptionally slow-growing and extremely cold hardy, adapted to harsh high-elevation conditions in its native range. Plant in full sun on well-drained soil, and be patient, since it can take decades to reach a modest mature size. Once established it needs very little care and tolerates cold, wind, and poor soil better than most ornamental pines.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into well-drained soil in full sun; this species tolerates heat, drought, and alkaline soil better than true arborvitae.

directions: Oriental arborvitae is the East Asian species behind the globe-shaped and golden named selections such as 'Franky Boy' already grown, bearing flattened, fan-like sprays of scale-like foliage arranged in distinctive vertical planes rather than the horizontal sprays of true arborvitae. Small, fleshy, blue-green cones with hooked scales are a distinguishing feature when present. Plant in full sun on well-drained soil; it is notably more heat, drought, and alkaline-soil tolerant than Thuja species, making it a good substitute in hot, dry climates. It takes shearing well for hedging or can be left to grow into its natural upright, irregular form.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall into well-drained soil in full sun; it naturalizes readily where conditions suit it.

directions: Tassel hyacinth is the Mediterranean wild-type species behind the frilled, sterile-flowered 'Plumosum' selection already grown as an ornamental curiosity, bearing an unusual two-part flower spike: a lower cluster of olive-brown fertile flowers topped by a showy tuft of sterile violet-blue ones resembling a tassel. It is taller and more architecturally unusual than common grape hyacinth, adding an eye-catching accent to a spring bulb border. Plant bulbs in fall into well-drained soil in full sun, and allow foliage to die back naturally after bloom to recharge the bulb. It naturalizes well in a sunny, well-drained border or rock garden over time.

subcategory: cool-season bedding and rock garden flower

planting.note: Sow in early spring or late summer into moist, well-drained soil; it prefers cool temperatures and declines in summer heat.

directions: Alpine forget-me-not is the European mountain wild-type species behind the deeper-blue named selections such as 'Bellamy Blue' already grown, forming a compact mound of small sky-blue, yellow-eyed flowers over hairy gray-green foliage. It is the more compact, cold-hardy relative of common woodland forget-me-not and is the official state flower of Alaska, reflecting its preference for cool climates. Plant in partial sun on consistently moist, well-drained soil, and expect it to decline or go dormant through hot, humid summers farther south. It self-sows readily in favorable conditions, often behaving as a short-lived perennial or biennial.

planting.note: Plant container stock in fall or spring into moist, well-drained soil in full sun, cutting old stems back hard every few years to refresh winter twig color.

directions: Common dogwood is the Eurasian wild-type species behind the fiery orange-and-yellow stemmed 'Midwinter Fire' selection already grown for winter twig color, bearing dark, maroon-red bark in its unselected form along with flat clusters of small white spring flowers and dark berries. Like its named cultivars, it colors best on young wood, so an annual or biennial hard pruning of a portion of the oldest stems keeps the display vivid. Plant in full sun to light shade on moist, well-drained soil, where it tolerates a range of conditions including occasional wet spots. It suckers over time to form a multi-stemmed thicket if left unchecked.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into cool, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade, sheltered from hot afternoon sun.

directions: Northern Japanese hemlock is a slow-growing, densely branched conifer from the mountains of Japan, bearing short, glossy dark green needles and a compact, pyramidal habit that suits it well to smaller gardens than many other hemlocks. It is notably more resistant to hemlock woolly adelgid pressure than the native eastern hemlock, making it a useful substitute where that pest is a concern. Plant in partial shade on cool, consistently moist, well-drained soil, avoiding hot, dry, exposed sites. It grows slowly into a dense, handsome specimen or screening tree with minimal pruning needed.

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped stock in spring into moist, well-drained soil in full sun, keeping roots cool with mulch.

directions: Japanese white birch is the East Asian species behind the chalk-white-barked named selections already grown as fast-growing ornamental specimens, sharing the same striking peeling white bark as paper birch with somewhat better tolerance of heat and the bronze birch borer that plagues many birches. Triangular, finely serrated leaves turn yellow in fall atop graceful, slightly pendulous branching. Plant in full sun on moist, well-drained, cool soil, and mulch to keep roots shaded, since birches dislike hot, dry root zones. It is relatively fast-growing but, like most birches, is not especially long-lived compared with other shade trees.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; tolerates heavy pruning and shearing well.

directions: Spreading euonymus is a tough, adaptable East Asian shrub grown mainly for dense, glossy evergreen to semi-evergreen screening and hedging, holding its leaves through most winters except the coldest end of its hardiness range. Clusters of small, inconspicuous flowers in late summer give way to orange-red berry capsules that split open attractively in fall. Plant in full sun to partial shade on well-drained soil of nearly any type, where it tolerates heat, drought, and heavy pruning with ease. It is commonly sheared into formal hedges but can also be left loosely pruned as an informal screen.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container stock in fall or spring into well-drained soil in full sun, pruning right after flowering to shape.

directions: Korean forsythia is one of the parent species behind several cold-hardy hybrid forsythia already grown, prized for flower buds that withstand harsh winters better than common forsythia, resulting in a fuller spring bloom even after severe cold. Bright yellow, four-petaled flowers open on bare stems before the leaves emerge, covering the arching branches in a solid curtain of color. Plant in full sun on well-drained soil, and prune immediately after flowering, since next year's buds form soon afterward on the current season's growth. It tolerates a wide range of soils and needs little care beyond periodic renewal pruning of old wood.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Direct sow or plant divisions in spring into moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun.

directions: Tutsan is a European and western Asian shrub grown both as a garden ornamental and historically as a wound-healing herb, producing clusters of small golden-yellow summer flowers followed by showy berries that ripen through red to glossy black, often cut for arrangements. Its common name derives from the French "tout-sain," meaning "all healthy," referring to its traditional use in herbal medicine. Plant in partial shade to full sun on moist, well-drained soil, where it tolerates both woodland-edge conditions and more open borders. It can self-sow and spread modestly, so remove unwanted seedlings if a tidier planting is desired.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade.

directions: Mochi tree holly is a slow-growing East Asian evergreen prized for its smooth-margined, glossy, leathery leaves lacking the spiny teeth typical of most hollies, along with bright red berries on female plants in fall and winter. Its bark is used in Japan to make a sticky birdlime once used for catching small birds, giving the species its common name. Plant in full sun to partial shade on well-drained soil, where it tolerates both coastal exposure and urban conditions reasonably well. It is naturally dense and tidy, needing little pruning to maintain a handsome, rounded form.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; it spreads wide and low, so space with room to fill in.

directions: Privet honeysuckle is a low, wide-spreading Chinese shrub grown for dense, fine-textured evergreen to semi-evergreen foliage rather than showy flowers, forming a mounded groundcover or low hedge useful on banks and slopes. Its tiny, inconspicuous creamy flowers in spring are followed by small translucent purple berries, both easily overlooked against the foliage. Plant in full sun to partial shade on well-drained soil, and prune lightly after flowering if a tidier shape is desired. It is relatively low-maintenance and tolerates a range of soil types once established.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant grafted or seedling stock in fall, setting the graft union a few inches below soil level, into well-drained soil in full sun to light shade.

directions: Osti tree peony is a wild Chinese tree peony species cultivated for centuries both as an ornamental and as the primary source of peony root bark and peony seed oil, bearing large, pure white, lightly fragrant single flowers in spring. It is one of the parent species behind many modern tree peony hybrids, valued for its vigor and relative ease of cultivation compared to some other wild tree peonies. Plant in full sun to light afternoon shade on deep, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil, and avoid disturbing the woody root crown once established. Like other tree peonies, the woody framework persists through winter and should not be cut back like herbaceous peonies.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, and install a root barrier, since this running bamboo spreads aggressively by rhizome.

directions: Green-stem bamboo is a fast-growing East Asian timber bamboo behind the golden-culmed named selections already grown, producing tall, thick, bright green canes densely clothed in foliage. Like other running Phyllostachys species it spreads vigorously and can become invasive without containment, so install a deep rhizome barrier or site it where unrestricted spread is acceptable. Plant in full sun to partial shade on moist, fertile, well-drained soil, and expect it to colonize steadily once established. Regular thinning of old canes keeps a grove looking tidy and promotes vigorous new growth.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

common_name: Chinese White Pear (Ya Pear, Wild-Type Species)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container stock in fall or late winter into well-drained soil in full sun, and plant a second genetically distinct pear nearby for pollination.

directions: Chinese white pear is the wild-type species behind the crisp, juicy, russet-skinned Ya pear and related Asian pear cultivars already grown, bearing round to pear-shaped fruit with a notably crunchy, apple-like texture rather than the soft, buttery flesh of European pears. The species is highly resistant to fire blight, a disease that devastates many European pear cultivars, making it a valuable rootstock and breeding parent. Plant in full sun on well-drained soil, and because most pears are self-incompatible, plant a second genetically distinct pear nearby to ensure good fruit set. Fruit is typically harvested while still firm and can be eaten immediately, unlike European pears that need a ripening period off the tree.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade.

directions: This compact Japanese evergreen azalea is the species long thought to be the key wild parent behind the Kurume azalea group, one of the most widely planted evergreen azalea lines in the American South, known for smothering spring bloom and small, glossy leaves. It forms a dense, twiggy, low-mounding shrub that responds well to shearing into a formal hedge or foundation planting. Plant in partial shade on acidic, moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil, since it shares the same shallow, fine root system and intolerance of wet feet as other evergreen azaleas. Light pruning right after bloom keeps plants dense without sacrificing next year's flowers.

planting.note: Plant container stock in fall or spring into well-drained soil in full sun, pruning right after flowering to renew growth.

directions: Reeves spirea is a long-cultivated Chinese shrub prized for its arching branches lined solidly with small, pure white double or single flower clusters in mid-spring, a classic pass-along plant in older Southern gardens. It forms a loose, fountain-like mound of fine-textured foliage that provides structure even after the bloom fades. Plant in full sun on well-drained soil, and prune immediately after flowering, since next year's buds form on the current season's growth. It is tough and adaptable, tolerating heat and a range of soils with minimal care once established.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container stock in fall or spring into well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun.

directions: Hungarian lilac is an Eastern European species valued for blooming slightly later than common lilac, extending the lilac season with dense, upright panicles of lightly fragrant violet-purple flowers against glossy, dark green leaves. It is notably resistant to powdery mildew and borer problems that trouble some other lilac species, and tolerates colder winters than many garden lilac hybrids. Plant in full sun on well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil, and prune immediately after flowering to maintain shape without losing next year's buds. It is a tough, reliable shrub for the coldest parts of its hardiness range.

planting.note: Plant container stock in fall or spring into well-drained soil in full sun, pruning right after flowering to shape.

directions: Early weigela lives up to its name by opening its rose-pink, funnel-shaped flowers one to two weeks ahead of most other weigela species and cultivars, giving it a useful place at the front of the spring flowering-shrub season. Dense clusters of blooms line the arching branches, drawing hummingbirds and other pollinators. Plant in full sun on well-drained soil, and prune immediately after flowering, since next year's buds set soon afterward on the current season's wood. It is a tough, easy-care shrub needing little beyond an occasional thinning of old stems to stay vigorous.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container stock in fall or spring on a sturdy, large structure in well-drained soil in full sun, since this is an extremely vigorous climber.

directions: Himalayan musk rose is the vigorous wild Chinese species behind the famous giant-growing selection 'Kiftsgate' already grown, capable of scrambling thirty feet or more into large trees when given the chance. Enormous sprays of small, single, musk-scented white flowers smother the plant for several weeks in summer, followed by a show of small red hips in fall. Plant in full sun on well-drained soil against a sturdy, large-scale structure or mature tree, since this is not a rose for a small trellis. It needs very little pruning or care once established, aside from occasionally reining in its considerable size.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into well-drained soil in full sun; it is sensitive to winter wet, so sharp drainage is essential.

directions: Whipcord hebe is the New Zealand species behind the popular blue-gray groundcover selection 'Pagei' already grown, carrying small, thick, glaucous leaves densely packed along low, spreading stems. Short spikes of small white flowers appear in late spring, but the plant is grown mainly for its neat, silvery-blue foliage and tidy mounded habit. Plant in full sun on sharply drained soil, since it is intolerant of wet, heavy ground, particularly over winter. It makes an excellent low edging or rock garden plant in climates with mild, well-drained winters.

planting.note: Direct sow or plant container stock in spring into lean, well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Silky-leaf broom is the European species behind the golden-flowered groundcover selection 'Vancouver Gold' already grown, forming a low, wide mat of fine, silky-haired stems that smothers itself in small bright yellow pea flowers in late spring. It thrives in lean, rocky, well-drained soil where richer plants would struggle, making it a dependable choice for a dry bank or rock garden. Plant in full sun on well-drained soil, and avoid rich or consistently moist ground, which encourages weak, floppy growth. It needs almost no supplemental water or fertilizer once established.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into well-drained soil in full sun; it roots as it spreads, helping it knit together quickly as a groundcover.

directions: Prostrate cotoneaster is the low, mat-forming species behind the vigorous named selection 'Queen of Carpets' already grown, hugging the ground tightly while spreading widely, rooting where its stems make contact with soil. Small white spring flowers give way to bright red berries in fall that persist into winter, attracting birds. Plant in full sun on well-drained soil, where it tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil well once established. It makes an effective, low-maintenance groundcover for banks and slopes where mowing is impractical.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring into sharply drained, gritty soil in full sun.

directions: Blue spruce stonecrop is the European species behind the named selection 'Blue Spruce' already grown, carrying needle-like, blue-gray succulent leaves on upright-then-trailing stems that resemble a miniature conifer more than a typical sedum. Clusters of starry yellow flowers appear in summer atop the foliage mats. Plant in full sun on sharply drained, gritty or sandy soil, and avoid rich or consistently moist ground, which encourages rot. It is extremely drought tolerant once established and spreads readily to form a dense, textural groundcover in a rock garden or dry border.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into moist, humus-rich soil in shade to partial shade.

directions: Hairy wood-rush is the European and Asian wild-type species behind the named selection 'Igel' already grown, forming a low, grass-like tuft of soft, hair-fringed leaves that brightens the shaded forest floor in early spring with small brown-flowered clusters. It tolerates the dry shade of established trees better than many fine-textured groundcovers, spreading gently to fill in bare patches beneath a woodland canopy. Plant in shade to partial shade on moist, humus-rich soil, and divide congested clumps every few years to maintain vigor. It pairs well with ferns, hellebores, and other shade perennials in a naturalistic woodland bed.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox
